text: This bridge is alive. Nobody built it out of wood, steel or concrete. It was grown, root by root, from a living tree, and unlike every bridge you have ever crossed, it gets stronger as it gets older. One scientific survey catalogued seventy-six of them in the hills of a single Indian state. In the next nine minutes: how you grow a bridge, why anyone would bother, the famous double-decker, and why the whole world may soon be watching these hills.

We're in Meghalaya, in India's northeast. Zoom in to the Khasi Hills, south of the capital Shillong, and you reach Sohra, also called Cherrapunji, about fifty-five kilometres away. Just to the west is Mawsynram. Directly to the south, the border with Bangladesh. These two small towns fight over one title: the wettest place on Earth.

Sohra averages about eleven thousand eight hundred millimetres of rain a year. Mawsynram averages a little more, which is why it usually takes the crown today. But Sohra still holds the records. Between August eighteen sixty and July eighteen sixty-one, it received about twenty-six thousand four hundred and sixty millimetres of rain. That is twenty-six metres of water in twelve months. July eighteen sixty-one alone brought about nine thousand three hundred millimetres, still the world record for a single month.

Now imagine you live in a village down in these valleys. Every monsoon, the streams turn into torrents. A bridge of wood or bamboo would rot in the wet and be swept away. Steel or concrete would be expensive, and steel rusts. So the Khasi and Jaintia people found another material. One that repairs itself.

That material is the rubber fig, Ficus elastica. This tree sends out aerial roots that grip steep slopes and bare rock. And its roots have one more trick. When two of them press together, they can fuse into one. Botanists call it inosculation. Roots that fuse become a network, and a network can carry weight.

Here is how a bridge is grown. Plant a fig on one bank of the stream. As its young roots appear, guide them across, often through hollowed trunks of areca palm, or along a frame of bamboo. When a root reaches the far bank, plant it in the soil. Then do it again, and again. Young roots are tied and twisted together, so they fuse. Over time, the scaffolding can rot away or be replaced. The roots stay. Some bridges were even trained with no scaffolding at all.

This is not quick. Estimates for how long a bridge takes to become usable range from about ten to twenty-five years. A study published in Scientific Reports in twenty nineteen found one bridge still not fully functional after sixty-six years. Builders add to the same bridge over decades, sometimes over generations. The person who starts a bridge may never be the one who finishes it.

A steel bridge rusts as it ages. A root bridge does the opposite. Roots under load thicken as they grow, so the bridge reinforces itself where it is stressed. Joints fuse and harden. A mature bridge can reportedly carry fifty or more people at once. The researchers called these bridges the only known example of people repeatedly and predictably using tree growth to build structures. Ages are rough estimates, but some are thought to be several hundred years old.

How many are there? That twenty nineteen study listed seventy-six living root bridges across the Khasi and Jaintia Hills. Most are short. Of the lengths measured, fifty-eight were under twenty metres. But they ranged from about two metres to fifty-two point seven metres. The longest known, over fifty metres, is near Rangthylliang, close to Pynursla. They are found from about fifty metres above sea level to around twelve hundred.

The most famous is in the village of Nongriat. Two root bridges, one stacked above the other, over the same stream. The decks are roughly twenty-four and eighteen metres long. The upper level was added after floods. It is often said to be around two hundred years old, though like every age here, that is an estimate. To reach it, you walk down from the village of Tyrna, past a long single root bridge and over two metal suspension bridges. It's the photo that made these bridges famous.

So who looks after them? The study grouped seventy-five bridges by caretaker. Twenty-five were maintained by a whole village. Twelve by a single family or person. Eight by a group of villages working together. Fourteen were unknown. And sixteen were not being looked after at all. A living bridge needs living people.

That is the danger. Floods, fires and landslides have destroyed bridges. Without care, others decay or grow wild. As concrete roads reach more villages, there is less reason to tend a root bridge, and after heavy tourist traffic, concrete has even been added to at least one of them. A bridge that took decades to grow can be lost in a few seasons of neglect.

Which is why this matters now. In February twenty twenty-two, India placed these bridges on UNESCO's tentative list as Jingkieng Jri, Living Root Bridge Cultural Landscapes. In January twenty twenty-six, India submitted the full nomination for the twenty twenty-six to twenty-seven evaluation cycle. The landscape stretches across more than seventy-five villages in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills. The nomination puts the living bridges at its core, with the villages and forest catchments around them as buffer zones. If it is approved, these would be World Heritage.

Want to see one? Come in the dry season, October to March. From Sohra, drive about twelve to fifteen kilometres to the village of Tyrna. From there, thousands of stone steps lead down into the valley, around three thousand five hundred by many counts. Allow about two hours each way. Past the double-decker, a trail continues to Rainbow Falls. Basic homestays in Nongriat let you stay the night and walk out fresh.

Two honest warnings. That climb back up is steep, and in the monsoon, heavy rain and landslides make the trails risky. And remember, you are walking on someone's living heritage. Stick to the path, follow local rules, and pay the small village fees. They help keep the bridges alive.

So here is the true scale of a root bridge. Ten to twenty-five years to grow. Hundreds of years of use. Seventy-six bridges counted, and every one depends on the people who care for it. Would you trust your weight to a bridge made of a living tree? Tell me in the comments. And subscribe to True Scale for more places that seem impossible.
